# Demand Letter — Trademark Infringement

## When to use this

Use this when another party is using the Kingdom's name, seal, device, or a
confusingly similar mark in a way likely to make people think that party is the
Kingdom, is affiliated with it, or is endorsed by it. This is the instrument that
stops impersonation, and impersonation is the injury the Kingdom is most likely to
suffer.

Trademark protects against confusion as to source. It does not protect against
mention. Before drafting, be certain the complaint is about confusion and not
about someone talking about the Kingdom in terms the Kingdom dislikes. Anyone may
use the Kingdom's name to refer to the Kingdom — to report on it, review it,
criticise it, or say they attended. In the Second Circuit that question is folded
into the ordinary likelihood-of-confusion analysis rather than treated as a
separate defence (*International Information Systems Security Certification
Consortium, Inc. v. Security University, LLC*, 823 F.3d 153 (2d Cir. 2016)), and
15 U.S.C. § 1115(b)(4) protects descriptive use of a term otherwise than as a
mark. A letter to a critic is a letter about the Kingdom's thin skin, and it will
be published.

Where the problem is a domain name registered in bad faith, go to
`udrp-complaint-outline.md` instead or in parallel; the administrative route
transfers the domain without a lawsuit.

## Before you send

- [ ] **The mark and its scope are recorded** in the Register of Rights: the mark
      as used, the goods or services it identifies, the date of first use anywhere,
      and the date of first use in commerce.
- [ ] **The registration position is known and stated accurately.** Registration
      number, register (Principal or Supplemental), classes, registration date,
      and whether a § 15 declaration of incontestability has been filed. Where the
      mark is unregistered, the claim is under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a) and depends on
      proving distinctiveness — do not cite a registration that does not exist, do
      not describe a pending application as a registration, and do not use the ®
      symbol on an unregistered mark. Use ™.
- [ ] **Priority is established.** The Kingdom's first use in commerce predates the
      recipient's first use, and there is a document proving it — a dated
      publication, an invoice, a dated capture, a specimen. Priority is the element
      most often assumed and least often provable.
- [ ] **The recipient's use has been captured** with all four artefacts and
      deposited in the Evidence Vault with its custody record
      (`05-EVIDENCE-AND-CHAIN-OF-CUSTODY` § 2), including the listing, the profile,
      the account handle and numeric identifier, and any domain registration
      record.
- [ ] **Any actual confusion has been documented in writing** — the misdirected
      email, the visitor who arrived at the wrong address, the donor who thought
      they were giving to the Kingdom — with names, dates, and the original
      messages preserved with headers. This is the single most valuable evidence in
      the file and it is routinely lost.
- [ ] **Nominative and descriptive use have been ruled out,** and the analysis is
      in the matter record.
- [ ] **The recipient is correctly identified** as a legal entity, with the
      registered agent where one exists.
- [ ] **The Kingdom knows which of the two demands it is making** — cessation, or
      cessation plus an accounting — and why. See the Notes below; this choice
      determines how the matter proceeds more than any other drafting decision.
- [ ] **The deadline is one the Kingdom will act on,** and the follow-up is
      calendared.
- [ ] **The Kingdom's own legal hold has issued** and the matter is open in the
      Enforcement Docket.

## The letter

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD — name, postal address, telephone, email]

[DATE]

VIA CERTIFIED MAIL, RETURN RECEIPT REQUESTED, AND BY EMAIL TO [ADDRESS]

[RECIPIENT LEGAL NAME]
[ATTN: NAMED INDIVIDUAL OR REGISTERED AGENT]
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY, STATE, ZIP]

Re:  Unauthorized use of the mark [MARK]
     U.S. Trademark Registration No. [NUMBER]
     Our reference: [MATTER REFERENCE]

Dear [MR./MS./MX. SURNAME]:

I write on behalf of Apex Kingdom ("the Kingdom") concerning your use of a
mark that is [IDENTICAL TO / CONFUSINGLY SIMILAR TO] a mark owned by the
Kingdom. I ask that you read this letter carefully and respond by
[DEADLINE DATE].

THE KINGDOM'S MARK AND ITS PRIORITY

The Kingdom has used the mark [MARK] continuously in commerce since
[DATE OF FIRST USE IN COMMERCE] to identify [DESCRIBE THE SERVICES — e.g.,
"religious and fraternal society services" / "educational services" /
"charitable fundraising services"]. The mark is registered on the Principal
Register of the United States Patent and Trademark Office as Registration
No. [NUMBER], registered [DATE], in International Class[es] [NUMBERS]. A
copy of the certificate of registration is enclosed as Exhibit A. [WHERE
APPLICABLE: A declaration of incontestability under 15 U.S.C. § 1065 was
filed and accepted on [DATE].]

That registration is prima facie evidence of the validity of the mark, of
the Kingdom's ownership of it, and of the Kingdom's exclusive right to use
it in commerce in connection with the services identified, under 15 U.S.C.
§§ 1057(b) and 1115(a). [WHERE THE MARK IS UNREGISTERED, SUBSTITUTE: The
Kingdom's rights in the mark arise from its continuous use in commerce since
[DATE] and the recognition the mark has acquired among the public it serves,
and are enforceable under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a).]

YOUR USE

[STATE WHAT IS BEING DONE, WITH DATES AND PARTICULARITY. FOR EXAMPLE:]

On [DATE] the Kingdom observed that you are using [THE MARK / THE
DESIGNATION "[RECIPIENT'S MARK]"] at [URL / LOCATION / PLATFORM] in
connection with [DESCRIBE WHAT IS OFFERED]. [DESCRIBE THE MANNER OF USE —
signage, listings, advertising, packaging, social media handles, domain
names.] Dated captures are enclosed as Exhibit B. The Kingdom's records show
its own first use in commerce predates your first use by [PERIOD]; evidence
of the Kingdom's prior use is enclosed as Exhibit C.

WHY THIS IS LIKELY TO CAUSE CONFUSION

The Kingdom's mark and your designation are [IDENTICAL / differ only in
[RESPECT], and are identical in sound, appearance, and commercial
impression]. The Kingdom's mark is [ARBITRARY / FANCIFUL / SUGGESTIVE] as
applied to these services and is therefore inherently distinctive. You offer
[SERVICES] to [THE SAME AUDIENCE / AN OVERLAPPING AUDIENCE] in
[THE SAME GEOGRAPHIC AREA / THE SAME ONLINE CHANNELS] through
[THE SAME CHANNELS OF TRADE]. [WHERE APPLICABLE: The Kingdom has already
received [NUMBER] instances of actual confusion, including
[DESCRIBE — e.g., "a donation of $[AMOUNT] sent to your organization on
[DATE] by a person who believed they were supporting the Kingdom"].]
[WHERE APPLICABLE: You adopted the designation after [DESCRIBE THE FACTS
SHOWING KNOWLEDGE OF THE KINGDOM — e.g., "attending the Kingdom's [EVENT]
on [DATE]"].]

The result is that ordinary members of the public are likely to believe that
your [ORGANIZATION / SERVICES / GOODS] are the Kingdom's, or are affiliated
with, sponsored by, or endorsed by the Kingdom. They are not. That is
trademark infringement under 15 U.S.C. § 1114 and a false designation of
origin under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a).

WHAT THE KINGDOM ASKS YOU TO DO

By [DEADLINE DATE], please:

1. Cease all use of [THE MARK / THE DESIGNATION "[RECIPIENT'S MARK]"] and of
   any mark confusingly similar to the Kingdom's mark, in connection with
   [SERVICES], in all media;

2. Remove the designation from [LIST: your website at [URL], your social
   media accounts at [HANDLES], your signage, your printed materials, your
   listings at [PLATFORMS], and your email addresses and domain names];

3. [WHERE A DOMAIN IS INVOLVED: Transfer the domain name [DOMAIN] to the
   Kingdom, or cancel the registration, at the Kingdom's election];

4. Confirm in writing that you have done so, and that you will not adopt or
   use the Kingdom's mark or any confusingly similar designation in the
   future; and

5. Preserve all documents and electronically stored information relating to
   your adoption and use of the designation, including correspondence,
   design files, marketing materials, sales and donation records, web
   analytics, and any communications concerning the Kingdom. This letter
   places you on notice that a dispute is reasonably anticipated, and your
   obligation to preserve such material has now attached.

[INCLUDE THE FOLLOWING ONLY IF THE KINGDOM HAS DECIDED TO PURSUE MONEY AND
IS PREPARED TO LITIGATE FOR IT — SEE THE NOTES:

6. Provide a full accounting of all revenue, donations, and other
   consideration received in connection with your use of the designation
   from [DATE] to the present, together with the records supporting it.]

[WHERE THE KINGDOM WILL PERMIT A TRANSITION: The Kingdom recognizes that
changing a name takes time. If you confirm in writing by [DEADLINE DATE]
that you will discontinue the designation, the Kingdom will allow until
[TRANSITION DATE] for existing printed materials and signage to be
exhausted, provided all online use ceases immediately.]

NOTICE

This letter constitutes actual notice to you of the Kingdom's registration
and of its rights in the mark. Any continued use after the date of this
letter is use with knowledge of those rights.

RESPONSE

Please direct your response to me at the address or email above by
[DEADLINE DATE]. If you are represented, please have your attorney contact
me directly.

The Kingdom would prefer to resolve this in correspondence. If it is not
resolved by the date above, the Kingdom will consider the remedies available
to it under the Lanham Act.

This letter is not a complete statement of the facts or of the Kingdom's
position, and nothing in it waives or limits any right, claim, or remedy
available to the Kingdom, all of which are expressly reserved.

Sincerely,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]

[WHERE THE SIGNING OFFICER IS NOT AN ATTORNEY: I am an officer of Apex
Kingdom and am not an attorney. This letter is sent by the Kingdom in its
own behalf as the owner of the mark described above.]

Enclosures:  Exhibit A — Certificate of Registration No. [NUMBER]
             Exhibit B — Dated captures of the use complained of
             Exhibit C — Evidence of the Kingdom's prior use in commerce
             [Exhibit D — Documented instances of actual confusion]
```

## Notes

### The likelihood-of-confusion elements the letter should establish

Infringement turns on whether ordinary purchasers are likely to be confused about
source, sponsorship, or affiliation. In the Second Circuit — which governs
Connecticut — the analysis runs on the *Polaroid* factors (*Polaroid Corp. v.
Polarad Electronics Corp.*, 287 F.2d 492 (2d Cir. 1961)). The letter does not
argue all eight, and should not read like a brief. It should establish, briefly
and factually, the five that carry the weight:

**Strength of the Kingdom's mark.** Where the mark sits on the distinctiveness
spectrum — generic, descriptive, suggestive, arbitrary, or fanciful
(*Abercrombie & Fitch Co. v. Hunting World, Inc.*, 537 F.2d 4 (2d Cir. 1976)) —
plus whatever commercial recognition it has actually acquired. A coined name is
inherently distinctive and the letter says so in one clause. A descriptive one
needs secondary meaning, and the letter must be honest about that rather than
assert strength it cannot support.

**Similarity of the marks.** Compared as encountered in the marketplace, in sound,
appearance, and commercial impression — not letter by letter. Say what is
identical and what differs, and do not pretend a real difference away.

**Proximity of the services and overlap of channels and audience.** Confusion
requires that the same people encounter both. State the shared audience, the
shared geography, and the shared channels — the same city, the same platforms, the
same congregational or charitable field.

**Actual confusion.** Not required, and the most persuasive thing in the letter
when it exists. One misdirected donation with a date and an amount does more work
than three paragraphs of argument. Quote it.

**The recipient's good faith in adopting the designation.** Where there is
evidence they knew of the Kingdom — they attended, they corresponded, they
followed the account — set out the facts flatly and let them speak. Do not
characterise them as a bad actor in the first letter.

Two factors the letter ordinarily omits: bridging the gap and consumer
sophistication. They rarely help a plaintiff at this scale and inviting argument
on them is pointless.

**One claim not to make.** Do not plead dilution under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(c). It is
available only to marks that are "widely recognized by the general consuming
public of the United States" — a national-fame standard that a regional religious
society does not meet, and asserting it signals to opposing counsel that nobody on
the Kingdom's side has read the statute.

### A demand to stop, and a demand for an accounting

These are different letters wearing the same envelope, and the choice between them
should be deliberate.

**A demand to stop** asks for cessation and nothing more. It is cheap for the
recipient to comply with, costs them no money, and lets them treat the matter as a
naming error rather than an accusation of theft. It resolves at a far higher rate
than anything else the Kingdom can send, often within days, and it obtains the
outcome the Kingdom actually needs — the impersonation ends. Where a transition
period is offered for signage and printed stock, the rate is higher still. This
should be the default, and for a small local infringer it should be the whole
letter.

**A demand for an accounting** asks the recipient to disclose and hand over the
revenue attributable to the infringing use, under 15 U.S.C. § 1117(a). It changes
the character of the matter entirely. It will nearly always be refused; it sends
the recipient to a lawyer on the day it arrives; it converts a naming dispute into
a monetary claim the recipient will now defend; and it makes settlement more
expensive and slower. Include it only where the use is commercial and substantial,
the recipient is solvent, and the Kingdom is genuinely prepared to litigate — which
means prepared to spend into six figures in federal court.

Two points of statutory mechanics worth knowing before choosing. Under § 1117(a)
the plaintiff need prove only the defendant's sales; the defendant must prove all
elements of cost or deduction claimed. And under *Romag Fasteners, Inc. v. Fossil
Group, Inc.*, 590 U.S. 212 (2020), wilfulness is not an inflexible precondition to
an award of profits, though the infringer's mental state remains highly important
to whether profits are awarded at all. So an accounting is genuinely obtainable —
it is simply expensive to obtain, and asking for it early costs the Kingdom the
cheap resolution.

### Why the NOTICE paragraph is there

Section 1111 of the Lanham Act denies profits and damages to a registrant who did
not display statutory notice with the mark — the ® symbol or "Reg. U.S. Pat. &
Tm. Off." — unless the defendant had actual notice of the registration. The letter
supplies that actual notice, in writing, on a dated and tracked delivery. From the
date of receipt, the monetary clock runs. That single paragraph is often worth more
than everything else in the letter, and it costs three lines.

It also does the wilfulness work that the copyright demand letter deliberately
avoids doing by accusation: the Kingdom does not need to call the recipient a
wilful infringer today, because if they continue after this letter the record makes
the point without adjectives.

### What was deliberately left out

**No damages figure and no threat of criminal referral,** for the reasons set out
in `cease-and-desist-copyright.md`. Counterfeiting is a federal crime
(18 U.S.C. § 2320) and it is not the Kingdom's to threaten in a letter seeking
money.

**No assertion of the Kingdom's sovereignty, jurisdiction, or authority over the
recipient.** The Lanham Act binds the recipient regardless of what they think of
the Charter, and that is the whole point. Nothing in the letter styles itself as
process, bears a seal implying judicial authority, or implies that the signer is a
law enforcement officer or an attorney (`01-LEGAL-POSTURE` § 4; Conn. Gen. Stat.
§§ 53a-130, 51-88).

**No demand touching lawful reference to the Kingdom.** The demand paragraphs are
drafted to reach use of the mark to identify the recipient's own services. They do
not, and must not, ask anyone to stop naming the Kingdom, reporting on it, or
criticising it. A demand that overreaches into protected speech is the demand that
gets screenshotted.

**No fee shifting threatened.** Section 1117(a) permits an award of attorney's fees
in exceptional cases — and it runs both ways, against the Kingdom as readily as for
it. Raising fees in a first letter invites the recipient's counsel to explain that
symmetry to them.
